title: Tomorrow, and the bare verb
goal: Talking about plans with the prefix حـ — and closing the biggest gap for foreign learners: when a verb takes بـ and when it has to stand bare.
bekal: building future sentences with حـ for every person
using the form without بـ after عايز، لازم، ممكن، بحب

dialogs.title: حوار — خطة الأجازة
dialogs.intro: Thursday afternoon. Budi and Mona sit in the cafeteria, talking about the long holiday coming next week.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: What are you going to do over the holiday?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: عايز أسافر. بس لسه مش عارف فين.
lines.id: I want to travel. But I don't know where yet.
lines.literal: want I-travel. but still not knowing where.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: لازم تشوف الأقصر وأسوان. ده مش اختيار.
lines.baca: laazim tishuuf il-U’ṣur wi Aswaan. da mish ikhtiyaar.
lines.id: You have to see Luxor and Aswan. That's not optional.
lines.literal: must you-see Luxor and Aswan. this not choice.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Can I go by train? Flying is expensive.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: Sure. The night train will get you there by morning.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: طيب. حاحجز بكرة إن شاء الله.
lines.id: Okay. I'll book tomorrow, God willing.
lines.literal: okay. I-will-book tomorrow if God wills.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: And how many days will you stay there?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أربع أيام. مش حاقدر أكتر من كده.
lines.baca: arba‘ ayyaam. mish ha’dar aktar min kida.
lines.id: Four days. I can't manage more than that.
lines.literal: four days. not I-will-be-able more than that.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: That's enough. You'll see the temples, the Nile, and the feluccas.
lines.literal: enough. you-will-see the-temples and the-Nile and the-felucca.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: I love going on boats. I'll definitely try it.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: وممكن تنزل النوبة كمان. ناسها تحفة.
lines.baca: wi mumkin tinzil in-Nuuba kamaan. nas-ha tuhfa.
lines.id: And you could go down to Nubia too. The people there are amazing.
lines.literal: and possible you-go-down Nubia also. its-people masterpiece.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: We'll see. First I have to finish studying.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.id: Don't worry. The exam isn't hard.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: إن شاء الله. حاذاكر كل يوم لحد الخميس.
lines.baca: insha’allah. hazaakir kull yōm lihadd il-khamiis.
lines.id: God willing. I'll study every day until Thursday.
lines.literal: if God wills. I-will-study every day until Thursday.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: بالتوفيق. ولما ترجع، حتحكيلي كل حاجة.
lines.baca: bit-tawfii’. wi lamma tirga‘, hatihkiili kull haaga.
lines.id: Good luck. And when you get back, you'll tell me everything.
lines.literal: with-the-success. and when you-return, you-will-tell-me every thing.

notes: **The prefix حـ marks the future, and it takes the place of بـ.** So بروح (I go) becomes حاروح (I'll go). You'll also see it spelled هـ — هيروح — and hear it either as a breathy ح or a lighter هـ; they mean exactly the same.
**The prefix حـ comes from the word رايح, "going".** Just as English wore going to down to gonna, Egyptian has worn رايح down to a single letter. The same path shows up in many unrelated languages.
**To negate a plan, put مش in front — no wrap.** مش حاروح (I won't go). It's the only verb form negated with مش, and now the reason is clear: حـ started life as an active participle, not a verb.

**The word لما means "when" (in the future), and the verb after it stands without بـ.** لما ترجع (when you get back), لما أخلص (when I finish). Egyptian doesn't use the future form after لما — just like English "when you get back", not "when you will get back".
**The word فلوكة is the wooden sailboat of the Nile**, and a felucca ride at sunset in Aswan is one of the few things in Egypt you really mustn't miss. The plural is فلايك.
**People say بالتوفيق before an exam, an interview, or an important trip.** The reply is الله يوفقك. A more casual cousin: ربنا معاك, and the lightest of all: يلا، حظ سعيد.

grammars.title: Future verbs with حـ
body: Building it couldn't be simpler: take the verb form without بـ and put حـ in front of it.
after: Look at the second column: the form **without بـ**, which until now only showed up after عايز and لازم, turns out to be the backbone of the whole system. It's used for the future, for commands, after لما, and after every helper word.
For firmer plans, people put رايح or ناوي in front of the bare form, as in أنا رايح أسافر بكرة. The difference is subtle, and beginners can ignore it.
The words أكيد (definitely), يمكن (maybe), and ممكن (possibly) go in front of a future sentence to set how sure you are: يمكن حاروح، أكيد حاروح.

grammars.title: When the verb goes bare, and when it gets dressed
body: This table is the heart of this unit, and maybe of the whole book. Copy it onto a small card and carry it everywhere.
after: The rule fits in one sentence: **بـ is used only when the verb stands on its own as the main verb**. As soon as another word leads in front of it, بـ drops off.

The number-one mistake of foreign learners is **عايز بشرب**. If you catch yourself doing it, remember that عايز is itself an active participle — the sentence already has a head and doesn't need a second one.

blocks.text: The word صحرا gave English the name Sahara, and واحة shares its ancient Egyptian roots with "oasis". As for أهرام, the pyramids: the singular هرم *haram* means that pointed structure and has nothing to do with the word حرام.

blocks.title: The night train south
items: The trip from Cairo to Luxor and Aswan takes about ten to thirteen hours by train, and the night train is the option Egyptians themselves use most.
To book: عايز تذكرة للأقصر يوم الخميس. To ask the departure time: القطر بيقوم الساعة كام؟ To ask the platform: رصيف نمرة كام؟
Useful lines at the station: ده القطر بتاع أسوان؟ and فيه أماكن فاضية؟ (are there any free seats?).

blocks.text: These sentences go from least certain to most certain. Notice that they're all built from the same verb form.

The last row deserves special attention. In Egypt, almost every promise about the future ends with إن شاء الله, and leaving it out sounds subtly arrogant. On the other hand, إن شاء الله is also sometimes used to soften a refusal — and learning to read which one is meant takes time.

exercises.prompt: Turn these into future sentences with حـ.
Fill in the blanks with the right verb form, with or without بـ.

items: What are you going to do over the holiday? (to a woman)
I want to travel, but I don't know where yet.
You have to see Luxor and Aswan.
I won't be able to stay more than four days.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: فين / مش / بس / عارف / عايز / أسافر

answers: حاروح المعهد. — هي حتسافر بكرة. — احنا حناكل بره. — هما حيرجعوا الساعة عشرة. — انتي حتذاكري بالليل.
حتعملي إيه في الأجازة؟ — عايز أسافر، بس لسه مش عارف فين. — لازم تشوف الأقصر وأسوان. — حاحجز التذكرة بكرة. — مش حاقدر أكتر من أربع أيام.
حتعمل إيه في الأجازة؟ — عايز أسافر بس مش عارف فين. — ممكن أروح بالقطر؟ — حاحجز بكرة. — مش حاقدر أكتر من كده.
wave: Tonight, say five plans for next week with حـ, then repeat all five with عايز. Feel the difference in the first letter.
